title: Testing Basics & Table-Driven Tests
summary: Go ships testing in the standard library: any function `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in a `_test.go` file is run by `go test`. The idiomatic way to cover many cases is a **table-driven test** — a slice of input/expected structs looped over with `t.Run`, giving you broad coverage with very little code.

subtopics.title: The testing package & go test
subtopics.explanation: A test lives in a file ending in _test.go, in the same package (or package foo_test for black-box tests). Each test is a function func TestName(t *testing.T). `go test ./...` compiles and runs them; a test fails only if it calls t.Error/t.Fatal — otherwise it passes. This convention is the foundation the table-driven pattern extends.

subtopics.title: Table-driven tests
subtopics.explanation: Instead of writing one Test function per case, define a slice of structs holding the inputs and the expected output, then loop over it. Adding a new case is a one-line change, and the cases read like a specification — the idiomatic Go structure this whole topic centers on.

subtopics.title: Subtests with t.Run
subtopics.explanation: t.Run(name, func(t *testing.T){...}) creates a named subtest. Each case gets its own name in the output, runs independently, and can be selected with `go test -run TestSquare/negative`. One failing case no longer hides the others — the natural pairing with a table of cases.

subtopics.title: t.Error vs t.Fatal
subtopics.explanation: t.Errorf records a failure but keeps running, so you see every failing assertion. t.Fatalf records the failure and stops the current test/subtest immediately — use it when continuing would panic (e.g. a nil you're about to dereference). Choosing correctly is what keeps a table loop reporting every broken case.

subtopics.title: Test helpers with t.Helper()
subtopics.explanation: Calling t.Helper() at the top of a helper function tells the testing framework to report failures at the caller's line, not inside the helper. This keeps failure messages pointing at the real test case, which is what makes shared assertions usable in a big table.

subtopics.title: Benchmarks & fuzzing
subtopics.explanation: func BenchmarkXxx(b *testing.B) runs the body b.N times so `go test -bench=.` can measure ns/op. func FuzzXxx(f *testing.F) generates random inputs to find edge-case crashes. Both share the same _test.go files as your unit tests, so the testing package covers correctness, performance, and adversarial input together.

foundations.overview: Testing in Go is not a third-party add-on — it is built into the language toolchain. You write tests in files ending in _test.go, declare functions named TestXxx that take a *testing.T, and run them with `go test`. The community-standard structure is the table-driven test: list every case as data in a slice, then loop over the slice with t.Run so each case is an independently-reported subtest. This keeps tests short, exhaustive, and easy to extend.
foundations.formalDefinition: A Go test is an exported-style function `func TestXxx(t *testing.T)` in a `_test.go` file that signals failure by calling methods on its *testing.T; a table-driven test enumerates cases as a slice of structs and executes each, typically inside a t.Run subtest.
foundations.whyItMatters: Tests are the safety net that lets you refactor and ship confidently. Because Go's testing tools are standard, every Go codebase tests the same way — table-driven tests are expected in interviews and in any production code review.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a table-driven test as a spreadsheet: each row is one scenario (inputs + expected result), and the test runner walks down the rows checking each. Adding a scenario is adding a row, not writing new code.
foundations.runtimePerspective: `go test` compiles your package together with its _test.go files into a temporary test binary and runs it. testing.T tracks failure state per test; t.Run spawns each subtest as its own goroutine-isolated execution so a Fatal in one subtest stops only that subtest, not the whole run.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Validating pure functions, HTTP handlers (via httptest), parsers, and business rules; CI pipelines run `go test ./... -race` on every commit.
foundations.businessImpact: A solid test suite reduces production incidents and lets teams ship faster with fewer regressions, which directly lowers the cost of change.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Table-driven tests make coverage cheap to extend, so engineers actually add the edge case instead of skipping it; named subtests make failures easy to localize.
foundations.performanceImpact: Tests themselves aren't a hot path, but benchmarks (func BenchmarkXxx) live in the same files and let you guard against performance regressions with -bench.
commonUseCases: Covering many input/output cases for a pure function
Subtests per scenario with t.Run for readable output
Benchmarks and fuzz tests alongside unit tests

commonMisconceptions.myth: You need a third-party assertion library to write Go tests.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The standard library is enough: t.Errorf/t.Fatalf plus reflect.DeepEqual cover almost everything. Libraries like testify are optional sugar.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A test passes only if it explicitly says so.
commonMisconceptions.reality: A test passes by default; it fails only if it calls t.Error, t.Fatal, or panics. There is no 'assert pass'.
t.Fatal stops the current test/subtest immediately (it calls runtime.Goexit); t.Error records the failure and continues so you see all problems at once.

checkpoints.prompt: When does a Go test pass?
options: By default, unless it calls t.Error/t.Fatal or panics
checkpoints.explanation: There is no t.Pass(). A test passes unless it signals failure via t.Error/t.Errorf or t.Fatal/t.Fatalf (or panics). An empty test body passes.

checkpoints.prompt: What happens after the first failing case if you use t.Fatalf inside the loop (no subtests)?
options: Only the first failure is reported; the loop stops
checkpoints.explanation: t.Fatalf stops the current test function immediately (via runtime.Goexit), so the loop never reaches cases 2 and 3. Use t.Errorf in table loops to see every failing case, or wrap each case in t.Run.

checkpoints.prompt: This test always passes even when Add is broken. Why?
options: The condition is inverted — it errors only when the answer is CORRECT
checkpoints.explanation: The assertion is backwards: it reports a failure when Add returns the correct value (5) and stays silent when it's wrong. Assertions should fire on the wrong condition: if got != want { t.Errorf(...) }.

debuggingLab.title: Only one failing case ever shows up
debuggingLab.symptom: The table test has several broken cases, but `go test` reports just one failure and stops.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: t.Fatalf calls runtime.Goexit, which terminates the entire TestParse function on the first failing case. The remaining cases in the loop never execute, so you only ever see one failure even when several are broken.
commonMistakes: Using t.Fatalf inside a table loop, hiding all but the first failure.
Not wrapping each case in t.Run, so cases aren't isolated.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Make the test report every failing case. Use t.Errorf (continue on failure) and isolate cases with t.Run.

theory.question: What is a table-driven test and why is it idiomatic in Go?
theory.directAnswer: A table-driven test enumerates test cases as a slice of structs (inputs + expected outputs) and loops over them, usually running each inside a t.Run subtest. It's idiomatic because it separates the test data from the test logic: you add a case by adding a row, coverage stays exhaustive, and each named subtest is isolated and selectable.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A pattern where cases are data in a slice and a single loop exercises them all.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To avoid copy-pasting near-identical Test functions and to make adding edge cases trivial.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Range over the cases; for each, call t.Run(name, func) and assert got vs want, using t.Errorf so all cases report.

theory.whyImportant: It's the expected Go testing style; interviewers look for it and so do code reviewers.
theory.realWorldExample: Testing a validation function across dozens of valid/invalid inputs by listing them as rows rather than as separate test functions.

nestedTopics.title: Subtests
nestedTopics.explanation: t.Run names and isolates each case, so failures are localized and you can run one with -run Test/case.

nestedTopics.title: Capturing the range variable
nestedTopics.explanation: Before Go 1.22, c := c (or passing c into the closure) was required so each subtest saw its own case; harmless to keep afterward.

followUps.question: Why t.Errorf rather than t.Fatalf inside the loop?
followUps.answer: t.Fatalf stops the whole test on the first failure; t.Errorf records it and continues so you see every failing case.

followUps.question: How do you run just one case?
followUps.answer: go test -run TestName/casename, matching the subtest name you passed to t.Run.

theory.question: What's the difference between t.Error/t.Errorf and t.Fatal/t.Fatalf?
theory.directAnswer: Both mark the test as failed. t.Error records the failure and lets the test keep running, so you collect all assertion failures. t.Fatal records the failure and stops the current test or subtest immediately by calling runtime.Goexit — use it when continuing would be unsafe, like after a failed setup you'd otherwise dereference.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Two families of failure-reporting methods on *testing.T.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Some failures are recoverable (keep checking), others make the rest of the test meaningless or unsafe.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Error sets the failed flag and returns; Fatal sets it then calls runtime.Goexit, unwinding deferred calls and ending the goroutine running the test.

theory.whyImportant: Misusing Fatal in a loop hides failures; misusing Error after a fatal setup causes nil-deref panics.
theory.realWorldExample: Use t.Fatalf when opening a fixture file fails (nothing else can run), but t.Errorf when comparing each field of a result so all mismatches show.

nestedTopics.title: runtime.Goexit
nestedTopics.explanation: What Fatal uses under the hood; it runs deferred functions then terminates the goroutine, which is why Fatal must be called from the test's own goroutine.

nestedTopics.title: Fatal in helpers
nestedTopics.explanation: Calling t.Fatal from a goroutine other than the test's doesn't stop the test correctly — Fatal must run on the test goroutine.

followUps.question: Can you call t.Fatal from a spawned goroutine?
followUps.answer: No — Fatal/FailNow must be called from the goroutine running the test; from another goroutine use t.Error and signal back, or the behavior is undefined.

theory.question: What are the semantics of t.Parallel(), and why did table-driven subtests historically need to capture the loop variable? How does t.Cleanup fit in?
theory.directAnswer: Calling t.Parallel() inside a subtest signals that it can run concurrently: it pauses that subtest and defers it until the parent test function returns, at which point all parked parallel subtests run together. Because subtests were deferred, before Go 1.22 the closure would capture the single shared loop variable, so by the time the subtests ran the variable held the last case — you fixed it with c := c to give each iteration its own copy. Go 1.22 changed range so each iteration gets a fresh variable, making the copy unnecessary. Parallel tests pair naturally with go test -race, which surfaces data races between concurrently running cases. t.Cleanup(func) registers teardown that runs when the test (and its subtests) finish, in LIFO order, working correctly even with parallel subtests.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The concurrency model for subtests plus the deferred-teardown mechanism.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Parallel subtests speed up slow, independent cases; Cleanup gives a reliable teardown hook that composes better than defer across parallel boundaries.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: t.Parallel() parks the subtest until the parent returns, then the runner resumes all parallel siblings together; t.Cleanup pushes functions onto a stack run at test end after all parallel children complete.

theory.whyImportant: The pre-1.22 loop-variable trap is a classic bug that made all parallel cases test the last input, and it's a frequent interview and review topic; -race synergy is what makes parallelism safe.
theory.realWorldExample: A table of integration cases each hitting a fake server calls t.Parallel(); with -race the suite runs cases concurrently and flags any shared-state races, cutting wall-clock time.

followUps.question: Why does a parallel subtest not run immediately when t.Parallel() is called?
followUps.answer: t.Parallel() pauses the subtest and returns control to the parent; the runner only resumes parked subtests after the parent test function returns, so they run as a group.

followUps.question: How do you share expensive setup across parallel subtests safely?
followUps.answer: Do the setup in the parent before spawning subtests, register teardown with t.Cleanup, and ensure the shared resource is safe for concurrent use or give each subtest its own copy.

theory.question: How do you test code with external behavior — HTTP handlers, clocks, and dependencies — deterministically, and what's the tradeoff of using testify versus the standard library?
theory.directAnswer: Test HTTP handlers with the net/http/httptest package: httptest.NewRecorder gives you a fake ResponseWriter to call your handler directly and inspect the recorded status/body, while httptest.NewServer spins up a real local server for end-to-end client tests. For time and other nondeterministic dependencies, inject an interface (a Clock with Now(), a repository, a mailer) and pass a fake implementation in tests, so behavior is deterministic and no real time passes. These fakes slot straight into table-driven tests as fields. On testify versus stdlib: testify's assert/require reduce boilerplate, but the standard library (t.Errorf/t.Fatalf plus reflect.DeepEqual and cmp.Diff) is genuinely enough and keeps dependencies minimal — most Go teams treat testify as optional sugar, not a requirement.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Techniques for making I/O- and time-dependent code testable through fakes and httptest, plus a view on assertion libraries.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Real network calls and wall-clock time make tests slow and flaky; hidden dependencies make behavior nondeterministic.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: httptest replaces the transport/writer with in-memory equivalents; dependency injection swaps real clocks/services for controllable fakes; assertions can be plain stdlib calls or testify helpers.

theory.whyImportant: Deterministic tests are the difference between a trusted suite and a flaky one, and knowing httptest plus injection is expected of backend Go engineers.
theory.realWorldExample: A handler that stamps time.Now() takes a Clock interface; the test injects a fixed clock and uses httptest.NewRecorder to assert the exact JSON body, with no real time or network involved.

followUps.question: NewRecorder or NewServer — which should I reach for?
followUps.answer: Use httptest.NewRecorder to unit-test a handler function directly and cheaply; use httptest.NewServer when you need to exercise a real http.Client, middleware, or the full transport round-trip.

followUps.question: How do you compare complex structs in assertions without testify?
followUps.answer: Use reflect.DeepEqual for simple cases or google/go-cmp's cmp.Diff for readable diffs and options like ignoring unexported fields — both work with plain t.Errorf.

scenario.question: A teammate's test passes locally but the function it tests is clearly buggy. How do you find out why the test is useless?
scenario.directAnswer: Suspect the assertion logic first: an inverted condition (asserting on the correct value), a comparison that never runs, or a missing assertion mean the test can pass regardless of behavior. Add a deliberately wrong case, run `go test -v -run TheTest`, and confirm it fails; if it still passes, the assertions are broken. Also check it's actually being compiled (right package, _test.go suffix, TestXxx name).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A false-positive test that never exercises the real failure path.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Backwards conditions, unreachable assertions, or comparing a value to itself silently always pass.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Go tests pass unless an assertion fires, so a never-firing assertion equals an always-green test.

scenario.whyImportant: A test that can't fail gives false confidence — worse than no test.
scenario.realWorldExample: if got == want { t.Errorf(...) } reports failure only when the code is right, so the suite is permanently green.

nestedTopics.title: Mutation check
nestedTopics.explanation: Temporarily break the function (return a wrong value); a good test goes red. If it stays green, the test is the problem.

nestedTopics.title: Coverage
nestedTopics.explanation: go test -cover shows whether the buggy code path is even executed by the test.

followUps.question: What tool systematizes 'break the code and see if a test fails'?
followUps.answer: Mutation testing (e.g. go-mutesting) automatically introduces faults and flags tests that don't catch them.

scenario.question: A test suite is flaky in CI: it uses time.Sleep to wait for work, calls a real third-party API, and mutates a shared package-level cache between tests. How do you redesign it for determinism?
scenario.directAnswer: Attack all three sources of nondeterminism. Replace time.Sleep with injected control of time — pass a Clock interface (or use synchronization like channels/sync.WaitGroup) so the test advances time or waits on a real signal instead of guessing a duration. Replace the real API with httptest.NewServer (or an injected client interface) so responses are local, fast, and controllable, including error cases. Eliminate shared global state by isolating it per test: construct a fresh instance in each test, or use t.Cleanup to reset it, so tests don't leak state into one another. Then run go test -race -count=1: -race catches the data races that shared mutable state causes, and -count=1 defeats the test cache so you get a true run.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A remediation of the three canonical flakiness causes: timing, real I/O, and shared mutable state.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Sleeps race the real work, network calls fail or vary, and global state creates order-dependent tests.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Inject a clock and wait on signals; swap the network for httptest/fakes; give each test its own state and reset via t.Cleanup; verify with -race and -count=1.

scenario.whyImportant: Flaky tests destroy trust in CI and get muted or retried, which lets real regressions through; determinism is the fix.
scenario.realWorldExample: A worker test slept 200ms hoping a goroutine finished; replaced with a done channel and a fake clock, plus httptest for the upstream call, it became instant and reliable under -race.

nestedTopics.title: Detecting order dependence
nestedTopics.explanation: go test -shuffle=on randomizes test order; if results change, tests share state that must be isolated.

nestedTopics.title: Why -count=1
nestedTopics.explanation: Go caches passing test results; -count=1 forces re-execution so a flaky test can't hide behind a cached pass.

followUps.question: How do you wait for async work without time.Sleep?
followUps.answer: Have the code signal completion (a channel, sync.WaitGroup, or callback) and block on that in the test; if you truly need polling, use a bounded retry with a deadline via a context, not a fixed Sleep.

followUps.question: How do you reset shared state reliably even if a test fails?
followUps.answer: Register the reset with t.Cleanup so it runs regardless of pass/fail (and after parallel subtests), rather than a defer that a Fatal in a helper might skip.

systemDesign.question: Design a testing strategy for a backend Go service. What layers of tests would you write and how would you gate them in CI?
systemDesign.directAnswer: Build a layered strategy. At the base, unit tests as table-driven tests cover pure logic and business rules cheaply and exhaustively. For HTTP handlers, use httptest (NewRecorder for direct handler tests, NewServer for full round-trips) and inject fakes for time and dependencies so they stay deterministic. Use golden files stored in testdata/ for large or structured outputs (rendered templates, serialized payloads), regenerated behind a -update flag and diffed otherwise. Add fuzz tests (FuzzXxx) for parsers and any code handling untrusted input to surface panics and edge cases, with the fuzzer persisting crashers as regressions. Add benchmarks (BenchmarkXxx) for hot paths and track them with benchstat to catch performance regressions. In CI, gate merges on go test ./... -race (catch data races), enforce a coverage floor on critical packages, and run -count=1 for a clean, cache-free result; run fuzzing and long benchmarks on a separate schedule rather than every PR.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A pyramid of complementary test types plus the CI policy that enforces them.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: No single test type covers correctness, integration, adversarial input, and performance; each layer catches a different class of failure.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Table-driven unit tests for logic, httptest for handlers, golden files for structured output, fuzz for parsers, benchmarks+benchstat for perf, and CI runs -race/coverage/-count=1 as gates with heavier suites scheduled separately.

systemDesign.whyImportant: A coherent strategy gives fast, trustworthy feedback and prevents both regressions and flakiness, which is what lets a team ship confidently.
systemDesign.realWorldExample: A JSON API service: handlers tested via httptest with injected clocks, the response serializer verified by golden files, the request parser fuzzed nightly, hot encoders benchmarked with benchstat, and PRs blocked unless go test -race passes and coverage stays above the floor.

followUps.question: How do golden files avoid becoming rubber-stamped?
followUps.answer: Regenerate them only via an explicit -update flag and require the resulting diff to be reviewed in the PR, so a changed golden file is a visible, deliberate decision rather than an automatic overwrite.

followUps.question: Why not run fuzzing on every PR?
followUps.answer: Fuzzing is open-ended and slow; run a short bounded fuzz in PRs if at all, and do longer campaigns on a schedule, feeding any discovered crashers back as fast seed-corpus regression tests.

coding.question: Write a table-driven test (with subtests) for a function ParseRange(s string) (lo, hi int, err error) that parses "lo-hi". Cover a valid range, a reversed range (error), a non-numeric input (error), and an empty string (error).
coding.thoughtProcess: The function has two success outputs (lo, hi) and an error, so each table row carries the input, the expected lo/hi, and a wantErr bool. I list four cases: a valid "3-7", a reversed "7-3" that should error, a non-numeric "a-b" that should error, and "" that should error. Inside each t.Run subtest I first compare (err != nil) to wantErr, because when an error is expected the numeric outputs are meaningless; I use t.Fatalf there so a mismatch stops that subtest. Only when no error is expected do I check lo and hi with t.Errorf. Using (err != nil) == wantErr keeps rows declarative without hardcoding error values.
coding.lineByLine: The cases slice defines four rows, each with a descriptive name, the input string, expected lo/hi, and a wantErr flag. The loop copies c (harmless post-1.22, required before) and opens a named subtest with t.Run so failures are localized. Inside, we call ParseRange and first assert that (err != nil) equals wantErr; a mismatch is fatal for that subtest because the outputs can't be trusted. When an error was expected we return early. Otherwise we compare both lo and hi against the expected values with t.Errorf, which records the failure but lets other subtests continue.
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) for k table rows — each subtest runs once.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(k) for the table of cases.

followUps.question: Why check (err != nil) against a bool instead of the exact error?
followUps.answer: It declaratively expresses 'this row should/shouldn't error' without coupling the test to the error's text; when the specific error matters, add errors.Is against a sentinel like ErrReversedRange.

followUps.question: How would you extend this to assert the specific error for the reversed case?
followUps.answer: Add a wantErrIs field holding a sentinel error and, when set, assert errors.Is(err, c.wantErrIs) so reversed vs non-numeric are distinguished, not just 'some error'.

coding.question: Write a table-driven test (with subtests) for a function `Divide(a, b int) (int, error)` that returns an error on division by zero.
coding.thoughtProcess: I need cases covering normal division and the zero-divisor error. Each case carries inputs, the expected quotient, and whether an error is expected. In each subtest I check the error expectation first (since on error the quotient is meaningless), then the value. t.Run gives each case a name so failures are localized.
coding.lineByLine: The cases slice lists three scenarios including the error case. For each, t.Run opens a named subtest. We compare (err != nil) to wantErr so both 'expected an error and got none' and the reverse are caught; t.Fatalf here is fine because on an error mismatch the value check is meaningless. Only when no error is expected do we compare the quotient with t.Errorf.
coding.timeComplexity: O(k) for k cases — each runs once.

alternativeApproaches.title: errors.Is for typed errors
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If Divide returns a sentinel like ErrDivideByZero, assert errors.Is(err, ErrDivideByZero) instead of just 'err != nil' to pin down the exact error.
alternativeApproaches.code: if !errors.Is(err, ErrDivideByZero) { t.Errorf("want ErrDivideByZero, got %v", err) }

alternativeApproaches.title: Parallel subtests
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Add t.Parallel() inside each t.Run to run independent cases concurrently, speeding up large tables (capture the range var first).

followUps.question: Why compare (err != nil) to a bool instead of checking the error directly?
followUps.answer: It cleanly expresses 'an error is/ isn't expected' for each row without hardcoding the error value; use errors.Is when the specific error matters.

followUps.question: When would you add t.Parallel()?
followUps.answer: When cases are independent and slow (I/O, sleeps); it runs them concurrently. Capture the loop variable first so each subtest sees its own case.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Keep tests in the same package for white-box access, or use package foo_test for black-box tests that only touch the exported API (good for documenting the public contract). Put shared fixtures and helpers in a testdata/ dir and helper files; testdata is ignored by the Go build.
productionDeepDive.performance: Run `go test ./... -count=1` in CI to defeat the test cache when you need a clean run; use -bench and benchstat to catch performance regressions, and -short to skip slow tests in quick loops.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Always run `go test -race` in CI — the race detector catches data races that table tests with t.Parallel() can otherwise surface intermittently. Remember t.Parallel() subtests start after the parent returns, so capture loop variables.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Make tests deterministic: inject clocks and randomness, avoid real network/time.Sleep, and use httptest for handlers. Flaky tests erode trust in the suite faster than missing ones.
productionDeepDive.observability: Use `go test -v` for per-subtest output and -cover / -coverprofile to see which branches your table actually exercises; gate merges on a coverage floor for critical packages.
productionDeepDive.security: Add fuzz tests (FuzzXxx) for parsers and input-handling code to surface panics and overflows on adversarial input; the Go fuzzer saves crashing inputs as regression cases automatically.

caseStudies.problem: Validate huge numbers of input/output combinations across packages like strconv and net.
caseStudies.solution: Pervasive table-driven tests with named cases and subtests.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Slightly more upfront structure for vastly easier maintenance.
caseStudies.lessons: Data-driven cases scale to hundreds of scenarios without code duplication.

caseStudies.solution: Table-driven tests with fake clients/clocks and -race in CI.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Building fakes is effort, but removes flakiness from real I/O.
caseStudies.lessons: Inject dependencies so tests are fast, deterministic, and race-checked.

keyTakeaways: Tests live in _test.go files as func TestXxx(t *testing.T) and run with `go test`; a test passes unless it calls t.Error/t.Fatal or panics.
Table-driven tests list cases as a slice of structs and loop over them — usually inside t.Run subtests so each case is named and isolated.
Use t.Errorf to record a failure and keep checking other cases; reserve t.Fatalf for when continuing would be unsafe, and call t.Helper() in assertion helpers.
Run CI with `go test ./... -race`, add benchmarks and fuzz tests in the same files, and keep tests deterministic by injecting clocks and randomness.
